q: Sales budgets are usually prepared product-wise, territory-wise and customer-wise mainly in order to:

options.A: Determine the cost of production of each product
options.B: Decide the credit period to be allowed by the suppliers
options.C: Fix the responsibility for achieving the sales targets on the respective areas and salesmen, and to compare the actual sales of each segment with its budget
options.D: Compute the amount of depreciation on the sales office assets

q: The research and development budget of an enterprise is characterised by the fact that it:

options.A: Is drawn up for specific research projects approved by the top management, the amounts being sanctioned for each project, since the outcome of research is uncertain and its benefits arise over a long period
options.B: Is derived from the production budget by applying a standard research cost per unit of output
options.C: Varies directly with the output in the same way as the direct material cost
options.D: Is prepared only after the results of the research have been obtained

q: The administrative overhead budget of an enterprise covers:

options.A: The wages of the workers engaged directly on production
options.B: The commission payable to the salesmen of the enterprise
options.C: The cost of power and lighting consumed inside the factory
options.D: The costs of general administration, such as office salaries, office rent, insurance, stationery and depreciation of office equipment, which are largely fixed in nature

q: A sale is made on credit in March and the cash is collected from the customer in May. The sale is recognised in the budgeted profit and loss account in March. In the cash budget, this sale will appear:

options.A: As a receipt in March itself, because that is when the sale is made
options.B: As a receipt in May, when the cash is actually collected, showing that the cash budget follows the timing of cash movement and not of income recognition
options.C: In neither March nor May, because credit sales are excluded from a cash budget
options.D: As a payment in May, when the customer is paid back

q: For preparing a cash forecast covering a long period, the adjusted profit and loss method of preparing a cash budget may be used. Under this method, the starting point is:

options.A: The projected net profit for the period, which is then adjusted for non-cash items, changes in working capital, capital receipts and payments, tax and dividends to arrive at the expected cash position
options.B: The closing cash balance of the previous year, without any adjustment
options.C: The total of the sales budget for the period
options.D: The amount of the share capital of the enterprise

q: During the preparation of the budgets, fresh market information leads to the sales budget being revised upwards. The immediate consequence for the other budgets is that:

options.A: No other budget is affected, because each functional budget is independent
options.B: Only the cash budget needs to be revised, the production budget remaining unchanged
options.C: The production, materials purchase, labour and cash budgets must all be revised correspondingly, because the functional budgets are interdependent and are coordinated in the master budget
options.D: The master budget is abandoned and budgeting is started afresh in the next year

q: A cash budget for a month shows an opening cash balance of Rs 25,000, estimated receipts of Rs 2,90,000 and estimated payments of Rs 3,50,000. The position at the end of the month will be:

options.A: An overdraft of Rs 60,000
options.B: A cash balance of Rs 35,000
options.C: An overdraft of Rs 35,000
options.D: A cash balance of Rs 65,000

q: The credit sales of an enterprise were Rs 3,00,000 in February and Rs 4,50,000 in March. Experience shows that 60% of the credit sales are collected in the month following the sale and the remaining 40% in the second month following. The cash to be received from debtors in April is:

An enterprise purchases materials on credit. Its credit purchases were Rs 2,40,000 in March and Rs 3,20,000 in April. It pays its creditors 50% in the month of purchase and the remaining 50% in the following month. The cash to be paid to creditors in April is:

For estimating its working capital by the components method, an enterprise expects to hold raw material stock of Rs 2,80,000, work-in-progress of Rs 1,20,000, finished goods of Rs 2,00,000, debtors of Rs 2,40,000 and a cash balance of Rs 60,000. Its expected current liabilities are creditors Rs 2,10,000, outstanding expenses Rs 70,000 and a bank overdraft of Rs 20,000. Its net working capital requirement is:

The estimated sales of an enterprise for the coming year are Rs 48,00,000. On the basis of past experience, its working capital is estimated at 15% of the annual sales. The working capital required is:
The current assets of an enterprise are Rs 21,00,000 and its current ratio is 3.5 : 1. Its net working capital is:

In a manufacturing concern, raw materials are held for 35 days, the work-in-progress remains in process for 15 days, finished goods are held for 20 days and debtors are collected in 40 days. Suppliers allow 30 days' credit. The length of the net operating cycle is:

options.A: 80 days
options.B: 110 days
options.C: 140 days
options.D: 65 days

q: An enterprise shows negative working capital because a part of its fixed assets has been financed out of short-term funds. The main danger inherent in this position is:

options.A: That the enterprise will have to pay more income-tax
options.B: That its fixed assets will depreciate faster
options.C: That it will be unable to sell its products in the market
options.D: A serious liquidity risk, because if the short-term lenders and creditors press for payment, the enterprise cannot convert its fixed assets into cash quickly enough to meet them

q: Where no cash discount is offered by the suppliers, trade credit obtained on the usual terms is a particularly cheap source of short-term finance mainly because:

options.A: Within the credit period allowed, no explicit interest is charged on the amount owed, while the goods received can be used or sold before the payment falls due
options.B: The amount owed to the suppliers never has to be repaid
options.C: Trade credit is provided by the Government at a subsidised rate of interest
options.D: Suppliers allow the buyer to fix his own date of payment, without any limit

q: Outstanding or accrued expenses, such as wages, salaries, rent and interest that have become due but have not yet been paid, help in financing the working capital of an enterprise because:

options.A: Such expenses are never required to be paid at all
options.B: The bank pays these expenses on behalf of the enterprise
options.C: The enterprise first uses the services concerned and pays for them later, so that the amounts remaining payable act as an interest-free short-term source of funds until the due date of payment
options.D: Accrued expenses are a part of the share capital of the enterprise

q: An enterprise borrows Rs 8,00,000 from a bank at 12% per annum interest, but is required to keep 10% of the loan amount as a compensating balance in its account with the bank, which it cannot use. The effective rate of interest on the funds actually available to it is:
In the cash credit system of bank finance for working capital, the 'drawing power' of a borrower means:

options.A: The total limit sanctioned by the bank, which the borrower may draw in full at any time
options.B: The amount of the borrower's own contribution to the working capital
options.C: The profit that the borrower is expected to earn during the year
options.D: The amount computed on the value of the security, namely the paid-for stocks and book debts, after deducting the prescribed margin, the actual drawings being restricted to the lower of the sanctioned limit and the drawing power

q: A letter of credit opened by a bank at the request of a buyer of goods is, in the context of trade and working capital finance:

options.A: A loan of cash advanced by the bank to the buyer for paying the supplier
options.B: A written undertaking of the bank to the supplier or beneficiary to pay against the stipulated documents, being a non-fund-based facility which assures the seller of payment and enables the buyer to obtain the goods
options.C: A guarantee given by the supplier to the buyer about the quality of the goods
options.D: A bill of exchange drawn by the buyer on his bank

q: The ageing schedule of the receivables of an enterprise shows, over successive months, a steadily increasing proportion of the total debtors falling in the oldest age groups. This trend primarily indicates that:

options.A: The quality of the receivables is deteriorating and collections are becoming slower, calling for stricter follow-up and possibly a tightening of credit
options.B: The sales of the enterprise are falling rapidly
options.C: The enterprise is collecting its debts faster than before
options.D: The suppliers of the enterprise have lengthened their credit period

q: Under the credit scoring system of evaluating a credit applicant, the decision to grant credit is taken by:

options.A: Visiting the applicant's premises in every case and forming a personal impression
options.B: Scoring the applicant on characteristics such as income, occupation, length of service and past payment record, by means of a statistical scoring model, and comparing the total score with a pre-determined cut-off score
options.C: Asking the other suppliers of the applicant for their opinion in every case
options.D: Granting credit to every applicant who applies for it

q: A stores item is classified as 'Vital' under the VED system of inventory control in a production unit. The correct stocking policy for such an item is that:

options.A: It should be stocked strictly according to its annual consumption value, like a low-value item
options.B: An adequate safety stock should be maintained so that a stock-out is virtually ruled out, even if the item is of low value, because its non-availability would halt production
options.C: No stock of it should be kept at all, to save working capital
options.D: It should be ordered only after the production has stopped for want of it

q: The chief use of FSN analysis in the management of working capital is to:

options.A: Fix the selling prices of the finished products
options.B: Determine the credit period to be allowed to the customers
options.C: Compute the depreciation on the stores items
options.D: Identify the non-moving and slow-moving items of stock so that they can be reviewed and disposed of, releasing the funds unnecessarily blocked in obsolete stock

q: Where an enterprise adopts just-in-time purchasing, receiving materials in small and frequent lots timed to the needs of production, the effect on its working capital is that:

options.A: The average inventory held and the funds locked up in stock fall sharply, provided the suppliers are dependable and the delivery lead times are short and reliable
options.B: The inventory held rises, because deliveries are made more frequently
options.C: There is no effect at all on the working capital
options.D: The enterprise must pay for the whole year's material in advance

q: Even though the physical volume of its production and sales remains unchanged, an enterprise will require more working capital when the prices of its materials and its wage rates rise, mainly because:

options.A: Its fixed assets become more valuable in the market
options.B: Its suppliers stop supplying materials to it
options.C: A larger amount of funds gets locked up in each unit of stock held and in the debtors outstanding, since these are valued at the higher prices
options.D: The period of credit allowed by its suppliers becomes longer

q: The net profit of an enterprise is Rs 3,60,000, after charging depreciation of Rs 55,000 and a loss of Rs 12,000 on the sale of furniture, and after crediting interest of Rs 15,000 received on its investments. The funds from operations are:
In preparing a fund flow statement, the proposed dividend is treated as a non-current liability. On this basis, the correct treatment of the dividend is:

options.A: Both the provision made and the dividend paid are ignored in the statement
options.B: The proposed dividend is shown as a source of funds
options.C: The provision for proposed dividend made during the year is added back to the profits in computing the funds from operations, and the proposed dividend of the previous year actually paid during the year is shown as an application of funds
options.D: The dividend paid is deducted in computing the funds from operations and is not shown elsewhere

q: An enterprise pays cash for purchasing the goodwill of another business. In its fund flow statement, this payment will be shown as:

options.A: An application of funds, being the acquisition of a non-current asset, namely an intangible asset
options.B: A source of funds, because goodwill increases the value of the business
options.C: An operating expense to be deducted in computing the funds from operations only, with no other entry
options.D: No entry at all, because goodwill is an intangible asset

q: The debentures of an enterprise are redeemed at a premium, the premium being charged in the profit and loss account. The correct treatment of this premium in the fund flow statement is:

options.A: The premium is shown as a separate source of funds
options.B: The premium is ignored altogether in the statement
options.C: Only the premium is shown as an application of funds, and not the amount of the debentures
options.D: The premium charged to the profit and loss account is added back in computing the funds from operations, and the total amount paid on redemption, including the premium, is shown as an application of funds

q: Preliminary expenses and share issue expenses written off in the profit and loss account during a year are added back in computing the funds from operations because:

options.A: They represent cash actually received during the year
options.B: They are only the writing-off of fictitious or deferred assets on which the expenditure was incurred in an earlier year, and no funds move out of the enterprise in the year of the write-off
options.C: They are a part of the dividend declared during the year
options.D: They increase the working capital of the enterprise directly

q: Underwriting commission, in connection with the issue of shares or debentures by a company, is:

options.A: The commission paid to underwriters for guaranteeing the subscription of the shares or debentures issued, being a cost of raising capital and of a capital nature
options.B: The commission paid to the selling agents on the sale of the products of the company
options.C: The brokerage paid by an investor for purchasing shares in the stock market
options.D: The commission charged by a bank for collecting the bills of the company

q: For a financial enterprise such as a bank or a non-banking finance company, the cash flows arising from the loans and advances made by it to its customers are classified in its cash flow statement under AS-3 as cash flows from:

options.A: Investing activities, in every case
options.B: Financing activities, in every case
options.C: Operating activities, since lending is its principal revenue-producing activity
options.D: No activity, because loans are not cash flows

q: Under AS-3, cash flows arising from extraordinary items, such as the proceeds of an insurance claim for a loss by fire, are dealt with in the cash flow statement by:

options.A: Omitting them from the statement altogether
options.B: Showing them always under operating activities, whatever their nature
options.C: Showing them always under financing activities
options.D: Classifying them as operating, investing or financing cash flows according to the nature of the item concerned, and disclosing them separately

q: In preparing a cash flow statement, cash flows arising in a foreign currency are to be recorded:

options.A: At the exchange rate ruling on the date of the balance sheet in every case
options.B: At the exchange rate on the date on which the cash flow occurs, and the unrealised gains or losses arising from changes in exchange rates are not cash flows
options.C: Only at the end of the year, after netting all the receipts and payments
options.D: At the rate at which the original contract was entered into, ignoring the actual rate

q: Which of the following qualifies as a 'cash equivalent' for the purpose of a cash flow statement?

options.A: Treasury bills with an original maturity of 91 days, held as a short-term investment of surplus cash
options.B: Equity shares of a listed company held as an investment
options.C: Government bonds with a maturity of five years held as an investment
options.D: The inventory of finished goods held for sale

q: An enterprise acquires the assets of another enterprise by issuing its own shares, and in another transaction converts its debentures into equity shares. In its cash flow statement under AS-3, these transactions are:

options.A: Shown as investing and financing cash flows at the values of the transactions
options.B: Shown partly as operating cash flows
options.C: Excluded from the cash flow statement, because no cash is involved, and disclosed elsewhere in the financial statements
options.D: Shown as a reduction of the opening cash balance

q: An enterprise transfers a part of its bank balance into short-term money market instruments which qualify as cash equivalents, and later transfers the money back into its bank account. In the cash flow statement, these transfers are:

options.A: Shown as an investing outflow and an investing inflow
options.B: Shown as a financing outflow and a financing inflow
options.C: Shown as an operating outflow and an operating inflow
options.D: Not shown as cash flows at all, because movements between items that together constitute cash and cash equivalents are a part of the cash management of the enterprise

q: Where an enterprise issues shares at a premium and the whole amount, including the premium, is received in cash, the source of funds to be shown in the fund flow statement is:

options.A: Only the face value of the shares issued, the premium being ignored
options.B: The total amount received, that is, the face value of the shares together with the securities premium, and not the face value alone
options.C: Only the amount of the securities premium
options.D: The market value of the shares on the date of issue, whether received or not

q: In a fund flow statement, the net increase in working capital during a period, as worked out from the schedule of changes in working capital, is shown:

options.A: On the application or uses side of the statement, a net decrease in working capital being correspondingly shown as a source of funds
options.B: On the sources side of the statement in every case
options.C: Only in the profit and loss account of the enterprise
options.D: Nowhere in the statement, since working capital changes are not funds flows

q: An important limitation of the fund flow statement is that:

options.A: It cannot be prepared from the published accounts of an enterprise
options.B: It shows the cash position of the enterprise on every day of the year
options.C: It is historical in nature, being prepared from two balance sheets, and it does not by itself disclose the cash or liquidity position of the enterprise, the details of the individual current items appearing only in the separate schedule of changes in working capital
options.D: It is not permitted to be prepared by any enterprise

q: Cost ascertainment, as distinct from cost estimation, refers to:

options.A: Predicting the probable cost of a job in advance, mainly for quoting prices and submitting tenders
options.B: Determining the actual cost of work already performed, collected from the cost records
options.C: Fixing in advance the cost that ought to be incurred under efficient working conditions
options.D: Comparing the actual cost of a period with the budgeted cost for the same period

q: From the following data, the cost of material consumed during a period is: opening stock of raw material Rs 45,000; purchases Rs 2,75,000; carriage inwards Rs 12,000; purchase returns Rs 7,000; closing stock of raw material Rs 60,000:
Under the HIFO (highest-in, first-out) method of pricing material issues, issues to production are priced at:

options.A: The highest price of the lots of material held in stock, so that the closing stock is left valued at the lowest prices
options.B: The lowest price of the lots of material held in stock, so that issues are charged out as cheaply as possible
options.C: The price of the lot most recently purchased, irrespective of the other lots in stock
options.D: A predetermined standard price fixed for the whole accounting period

q: The annual demand for a material is 6,000 units. The cost of placing an order is Rs 75 and the purchase price is Rs 50 per unit. The carrying cost is 20% per annum of the purchase price. Using EOQ = sqrt(2AO/C), the Economic Order Quantity is:

options.A: 212 units
options.B: 424 units
options.C: 600 units
options.D: 300 units

q: Unit (single output) costing is most suitably applied in concerns which:

options.A: Undertake work strictly according to each customer's separate specification
options.B: Produce a single homogeneous product continuously, such as mines, quarries and brick kilns
options.C: Pass their product through a number of distinct processes before completion
options.D: Render services measured in composite units such as passenger-kilometres

q: The standard variable overhead rate of a department is Rs 12 per hour and the standard hours for the actual output are 4,000. Actual hours worked are 4,400 and the actual variable overheads incurred are Rs 54,000. The variable overhead cost variance is:

options.A: Rs 6,000 (Adverse)
options.B: Rs 1,200 (Adverse)
options.C: Rs 4,800 (Adverse)
options.D: Rs 6,000 (Favourable)

q: Under the standard price method of pricing material issues:

options.A: Issues are priced at the actual purchase price of the oldest lot in stock
options.B: Issues are priced at the current market (replacement) price ruling on the date of issue
options.C: Issues are priced at a predetermined standard price, and the difference between the actual purchase price and the standard price is isolated as a price variance
options.D: Issues are priced by adding a fixed percentage to the cost price to cover normal wastage in stores

q: Under the Priestman group bonus scheme, the time wages of a group of workers for a week are Rs 40,000. The standard output for the week is 5,000 units, but the group actually produces 6,000 units. The total wages payable to the group for the week are:
In the collection of factory overheads, 'standing order numbers' are:

options.A: The serial numbers allotted to customers' orders when they are received by the factory
options.B: Numbers allotted to each item or source of indirect expenditure, against which overhead costs are collected and classified
options.C: The code numbers allotted to machines for the purpose of computing the machine hour rate
options.D: The numbers allotted to stores items in the priced stores ledger

q: The sales budget of a firm provides for the sale of 8,000 units at Rs 55 per unit. Actual sales are 9,500 units at Rs 52 per unit. The total sales variance, computed on the value (turnover) basis, is:

options.A: Rs 54,000 (Favourable)
options.B: Rs 82,500 (Favourable)
options.C: Rs 28,500 (Adverse)
options.D: Rs 54,000 (Adverse)

q: A 'current standard' in standard costing is a standard which:

options.A: Is set at the level attainable under perfect working conditions, with no allowance for normal wastage or idle time
options.B: Remains unchanged over a long period and is used only to measure trends in costs over the years
options.C: Is fixed once for all by the costing manual and is never revised thereafter
options.D: Is based on current working conditions and prices, and remains in force only for a short period, being revised as conditions change

q: A worker is paid a piece rate of Rs 15 per unit for the units accepted as good. In a week he produces 320 units, of which 20 units are rejected as defective owing to his own fault. His earnings for the week are:
An essential requirement for the successful installation of a costing system in a factory is that:

options.A: The system should be designed to suit the nature, size and working methods of the particular business, and introduced with the cooperation of the departments concerned
options.B: A ready-made system working successfully in another factory should be adopted without any change
options.C: The costing department should work in complete isolation from the production departments
options.D: The maximum possible number of forms and returns should be introduced from the very beginning

q: From the following data for a period, the cost of sales is: raw material consumed Rs 4,00,000; direct labour Rs 2,00,000; direct expenses Rs 40,000; factory overheads Rs 1,60,000; opening work-in-progress Rs 60,000; closing work-in-progress Rs 40,000; administration overheads Rs 1,10,000; opening stock of finished goods Rs 70,000; closing stock of finished goods Rs 50,000; selling and distribution overheads Rs 50,000:
The main purpose of an idle time card in a factory is to:

options.A: Record the time at which each worker enters and leaves the factory gate
options.B: Record the time spent by each worker on each job and operation performed by him
options.C: Fix the standard time allowed for each job undertaken in the factory
options.D: Record separately, under its cause, the time for which workers were paid but no production took place, so that idle time can be analysed and controlled

q: The contract price of a work is Rs 60,00,000. The value of work certified is Rs 24,00,000, that is, 40% of the contract price, and the notional profit on the contract to date is Rs 1,35,000. Cash received from the contractee is 80% of the work certified. Using the rule applicable where work certified is between one-fourth and one-half of the contract price, the profit to be credited to the Profit and Loss Account is:
Under the base stock method of pricing material issues, the base stock, being a fixed minimum quantity of material always held in stores, is:

options.A: Treated practically as a fixed asset and always valued at the price at which it was first received, issues above the base quantity being priced on the FIFO or a similar basis
options.B: Revalued at the current market price at the end of every accounting period
options.C: Written off entirely to production in the year in which it is first created
options.D: Valued at the highest price paid for any lot during the year

q: Under activity-based costing, the machine set-up cost pool of a plant is Rs 3,60,000 for 1,800 set-ups and the quality inspection cost pool is Rs 1,40,000 for 2,800 inspections. A product requires 250 set-ups and 400 inspections. The total overhead cost assigned to the product is:

In a factory, overtime has to be worked because production was held up by a flood and a breakdown of power supply, both abnormal circumstances. The overtime premium payable for this work should be charged to:

options.A: The jobs on which the workers happened to be engaged during the overtime hours
options.B: The factory overheads of the period, to be absorbed by all jobs of the period
options.C: The customer who placed the largest order during that week
options.D: The Costing Profit and Loss Account, as an abnormal loss

q: The budgeted sales of two products are: A — 4,000 units and B — 2,000 units, the standard margins being Rs 25 per unit for A and Rs 15 per unit for B. The total quantity actually sold is 6,600 units. The sales quantity variance, computed on the margin basis, is:

options.A: Rs 13,000 (Favourable)
options.B: Rs 10,000 (Favourable)
options.C: Rs 3,000 (Favourable)
options.D: Rs 15,000 (Favourable)

q: In the three-variance method of analysing the total overhead variance, the total overhead variance is analysed into:

options.A: Material price variance, material usage variance and material mix variance
options.B: Labour rate variance, labour efficiency variance and idle time variance
options.C: Spending (budget) variance, efficiency variance and idle capacity (volume) variance
options.D: Sales price variance, sales volume variance and sales mix variance

q: In a process, the opening work-in-progress is 1,000 units. During the period 6,000 units are completed and transferred to the next process, and the closing work-in-progress is 1,500 units, which are 40% complete as to conversion cost. The equivalent production in respect of conversion cost, computed under the average (weighted average) cost method, is:

options.A: 6,000 units
options.B: 6,600 units
options.C: 7,500 units
options.D: 6,300 units

q: In contract costing, plant that was issued to a contract site is returned to stores during the year. The Contract Account is credited with:

options.A: The original cost of the plant when it was purchased
options.B: Nil, because plant once charged to a contract is never credited back
options.C: The estimated scrap value of the plant at the end of its life
options.D: The written-down (depreciated) value of the plant on the date of its return

q: The expected selling price of a new product is Rs 950 per unit and the firm requires a profit margin of 20% on the selling price. The cost of the product, as presently estimated, is Rs 835 per unit. The target cost gap to be eliminated before the product is launched is:

options.A: Rs 75 per unit
options.B: Rs 115 per unit
options.C: Rs 190 per unit
options.D: Rs 60 per unit

q: A duration driver, as distinct from a transaction driver, in activity-based costing measures:

options.A: The number of times an activity is performed, such as the number of purchase orders placed
options.B: The total cost of the resources consumed by the activity during the period
options.C: The amount of time taken to perform the activity, such as set-up hours, rather than merely the number of times the activity occurs
options.D: The selling value of the output for which the activity is performed

q: The closing stock of a receiving process is valued at Rs 90,000. The output was transferred to it by the earlier process at cost plus 25% on cost. The unrealised profit included in the closing stock, for which a stock reserve is to be created, is:

A product line shows: sales Rs 6,00,000; variable costs Rs 3,90,000; fixed costs specifically attributable to the line and avoidable if it is dropped Rs 1,50,000; allocated common fixed costs Rs 1,10,000; and a reported net loss of Rs 50,000. If the line is dropped, the total profit of the firm will:

options.A: Increase by Rs 50,000
options.B: Decrease by Rs 2,10,000
options.C: Remain unchanged
options.D: Decrease by Rs 60,000

q: 'Generic benchmarking', as a technique of performance improvement, involves:

options.A: Comparing a business process with the best practice of that process wherever it is found, even in a completely unrelated industry
options.B: Comparing the performance of one department or unit with another unit of the same organisation
options.C: Comparing the firm's products and costs only with those of its direct competitors
options.D: Comparing a function of the firm with the same function in another firm of the same industry

q: The estimated works cost of a job is Rs 3,00,000. Office and administration overheads are to be recovered at 10% of works cost, and a profit of 20% on the selling price is required. The price to be quoted for the job is:
In contract costing, the amounts paid to sub-contractors for work executed by them as part of the main contract are:

options.A: Treated as a part of the cost of materials issued to the contract
options.B: Debited directly to the Contract Account as a charge for work done on the contract
options.C: Borne by the main contractor personally and not charged to the contract at all
options.D: Apportioned as general overheads over all the contracts in hand

q: Pareto analysis, as applied to inventory control and cost control, is based on the observation that:

options.A: All items of stores contribute equally to the total value of inventory
options.B: Total cost increases in a straight line with the level of output
options.C: Defects in production occur evenly over all products and processes
options.D: A small proportion of the items accounts for a large proportion of the total value, the 'vital few', while the remaining large number of items accounts for only a small proportion, the 'trivial many'

q: A contract is nearing completion. The contract price is Rs 80,00,000 and the estimated total cost of the contract is Rs 68,00,000. The value of work certified is Rs 60,00,000 and cash received from the contractee is Rs 54,00,000. On the estimated profit basis, the profit to be credited to the Profit and Loss Account is:
The first unit of a new product takes 400 labour hours. The learning rate is 90%. The cumulative average labour time per unit for the first four units is:

options.A: 360 hours
options.B: 400 hours
options.C: 324 hours
options.D: 288 hours

q: Under the reverse cost method of accounting for a by-product, the value at which the by-product is credited to the process account is arrived at by:

options.A: Adding the estimated profit margin to the cost of further processing of the by-product
options.B: Deducting from the sales value of the by-product the estimated profit margin on it, its selling and distribution expenses and the cost of its further processing after the split-off point, and crediting the net amount to the process
options.C: Crediting the full gross sales value of the by-product to the process account without any deduction
options.D: Ignoring the by-product altogether until the whole of it is sold

q: A firm sells two products in a constant sales mix (by value): Product A — sales Rs 4,00,000 with a P/V ratio of 50%, and Product B — sales Rs 6,00,000 with a P/V ratio of 30%. Total fixed costs are Rs 5,70,000. The overall break-even sales of the firm are:
The method of least squares, used for segregating a semi-variable cost into its fixed and variable elements, is regarded as the most accurate statistical method because it:

options.A: Fits the cost line by using all the observations and minimising the sum of the squares of the deviations of the observations from that line
